locations.name: CENTRAL JAIL - MAIN GATE
locations.description: The main entrance to the Central Jail, an imposing and fortified structure.
locations.architectureCues: A high wall the colour of old bone, topped with broken glass and rusted wire. A watchtower. A black iron gate set into the wall like a mouth. Above it, faded government seal and motto.

locations.name: JAIL - INTAKE ROOM
locations.description: The processing room for new prisoners upon their arrival at the jail.
locations.architectureCues: A bare room. A ceiling fan pushing hot air in circles. A long counter, behind it a Head Clerk with a ledger and a stamp pad.

locations.name: JAIL - INTAKE / STRIP AREA
locations.description: An area within the jail where new prisoners are required to strip and change into prison uniforms.

locations.name: JAIL - CORRIDOR
locations.description: A long gallery within the jail, lined with cell doors.
locations.architectureCues: A long gallery with cell doors and bars.

locations.name: JAIL - BARRACK
locations.description: A large communal cell or dormitory for multiple prisoners.
locations.architectureCues: A long hall. Maybe thirty men. Bedrolls in rows, a stinking corner latrine, a barred window throwing bars of light across the concrete. The heat sits on everything like a hand.

scenes.slugline: EXT. CENTRAL JAIL - MAIN GATE - DAY
scenes.summary: A prison bus grinds to a halt at the imposing Central Jail main gate, which groans open to swallow the bus and its new arrivals.
scenes.dramaticPurpose: Establishes the setting and the oppressive atmosphere of the jail. Introduces the theme of confinement and the start of the protagonist's journey into the prison system.

scenes.summary: New prisoners, including The Convict, are processed in a bare intake room. The Havaldar and Head Clerk humiliate The Convict by loudly announcing his charges (kidnapping, rape, murder) and assigning him a number (613) instead of his name.
scenes.dramaticPurpose: Introduces The Convict and his alleged crimes, immediately establishing him as an outcast. Shows the dehumanizing process of incarceration and the power dynamics within the jail system. Introduces key antagonist (Havaldar) and supporting character (Head Clerk).

scenes.slugline: INT. JAIL - INTAKE / STRIP AREA - CONTINUOUS
scenes.summary: The Convict is forced to strip and change into a coarse grey uniform. He secretly transfers a small, hard lump from the seam of his old collar into his closed fist, hiding it from the Havaldar.
scenes.dramaticPurpose: Highlights The Convict's vulnerability and introduces a mysterious element (the hidden lump), suggesting he has a secret or a plan. Reinforces the oppressive surveillance of the jail and the need for secrecy.

scenes.summary: The Havaldar marches The Convict down a long corridor, explaining the harsh hierarchy of the jail and warning him that rapists are particularly despised, even by other prisoners, before shoving him into the barrack.
scenes.dramaticPurpose: Further establishes the brutal rules and social hierarchy of the jail. Isolates The Convict by highlighting the specific contempt for his alleged crimes, setting up future conflicts. Transitions him to his living quarters.

scenes.summary: The Convict enters the barrack, where he is immediately targeted by Dagdu, the barrack kingpin, who, after hearing his charges from a Trusty, assigns him the worst spot by the latrine. Ganpat, an old prisoner, offers a quiet word of caution against judging based on rumors.
scenes.dramaticPurpose: Introduces the internal power structure of the barrack and the main antagonist (Dagdu) within the prison population. Establishes The Convict's immediate low status and the hostility he faces. Introduces a potential ally or observer (Ganpat) who questions the narrative.

verbal: Bangru Haryanvi dialect with regional rhythm, not generic Hindi polish
Use सै not है, के not क्या, म्हारा/थारा, कोन्या for negation
Honorifics: bhaiya, kaka, tau, chacha used by rank and age
Kinship framing even among strangers (beta, puttar, bhai)
Blunt humor, teasing, and dry sarcasm under pressure — rework jokes, not transliterate
Code-switching: official jail paperwork Hindi/English vs street Bangru
Idioms around izzat, laaj, dharam, kheti metaphors where natural
nonverbal: Direct eye contact as challenge; looking down as submission
Palm shove, shoulder push, matching stick rhythm for authority
Sitting cross-legged on floor; raised charpai for power
Silence used as threat more than volume
Greeting with nod or 'Ram Ram' among elders; none for convicts
wardrobe: Khaki police kurta-pyjama / shirt with brass buttons for havaldar
Coarse grey jail uniform, stamped number placard
Older inmates: torn vest, gamcha, rubber chappals
Power inmate: open shirt, matchstick, tin trunk near bedroll
Clerk: faded white shirt, steel watch, ledger ink stains
architecture: Bone-coloured plaster walls, rusted iron gates, broken glass on walls
Ceiling fans, bare bulbs, barred windows throwing stripe light
Concrete barracks, stinking corner latrine, muster yard dust
Rural Haryana cues: neem shade outside walls, tractor road dust, peepal near compound
food: Jail mess: watery dal, thick roti, onion, watery chai in steel tumblers
Trusty privileges: extra roti, jaggery, bidis
socialRules: Barrack hierarchy: who sits raised, who sleeps near latrine
Crime type determines izzat; sexual crimes mark someone as below the rest
Elders (kaka) can show mercy without losing face
Guards speak down; convicts do not answer back
humor: Mockery of the newcomer as entertainment
Laughing at paperwork ritual while enforcing it
